opus-5.5.text:
I think coding matters for a few reasons, and they reinforce each other.

The first is practical: code is one of the few domains where you get a very clean feedback signal. You write a program, you run it, and the tests either pass or they don't. For reinforcement learning, that's incredibly valuable. In many other tasks, like writing an essay or giving advice, judging what counts as "good" is fuzzy and you end up relying on human preference or another model as a judge. With code, the environment itself tells you whether you succeeded. That makes it a natural place to push reasoning and long-horizon behavior.

The second reason is that coding is a kind of universal interface. If a model can write and execute code, it can reach almost everything in the digital world: call APIs, manipulate data, operate tools, even build new tools for itself. I often think of coding less as one application and more as the model's hands. Once you can code, a lot of other agentic tasks reduce to coding problems.

The third is economic. Software engineering is a huge, high-value activity, and the people doing it are early adopters who are very willing to try new tools. You get real usage, real feedback, and a fast iteration loop between research and product. That loop is really important, because you learn what actually breaks in the real world rather than only on benchmarks.

And finally, there's something deeper. Real software tasks are long and messy. You need to read a large codebase, form a plan, try things, debug, and recover from mistakes. Those are exactly the capabilities we want from general agents: planning, memory, self-correction, working over many steps. So coding is a testbed where progress on "being a good coder" and progress on "being a generally capable agent" end up being very closely aligned.

So for me it's not that coding is the end goal. It's that it's the place where the signal is clearest, the leverage is highest, and the skills transfer most broadly.

fable-5.1.text:
I think coding sits at a very special intersection. On one side, it's one of the most economically valuable things a language model can do right now. Almost every company, every research lab, every piece of software in the world is built on code, so if you can meaningfully speed up or automate that process, the leverage is enormous. On the other side, and this is what excites me more as a researcher, coding is close to a perfect testbed for studying intelligence and agency.

Let me explain what I mean. When I was working on things like ReAct and later on agent benchmarks, the hardest question was always: how do you know whether the agent actually did the task? In a lot of domains, that's fuzzy. Writing a good essay, giving good advice, those don't have clean ground truth. Code is different. You can run it. There are tests, there are compilers, there are error messages. The environment talks back to you. That means you get a real feedback signal, and that signal lets you do things like reinforcement learning at scale, because you can verify outcomes instead of just imitating human text.

The second thing is that coding naturally forces long-horizon behavior. A real software task isn't one prompt, one answer. You have to read the codebase, form a plan, make changes, run things, see what breaks, go back and fix it. That loop of reasoning and acting, with observations coming back from the environment, is exactly what we mean when we talk about agents. So if a model can do that well in code, you've learned something general about how to build systems that can operate over many steps, recover from mistakes, and use tools.

The third point is that code is a kind of universal interface. If a model can write code, it can in principle control almost anything: call APIs, manipulate data, drive a browser, run experiments. In a sense, coding is the action space that connects a language model to the rest of the digital world. That's why I think of it less as one application among many, and more as the foundation layer for agents in general.

And there's a reflexive aspect that I find really interesting. The people building these models are themselves writing code all the time. So improvements in coding ability directly feed back into how fast AI research itself can move. If models become genuinely good at research-level engineering, that changes the pace of the whole field. That's a big part of why I think, if you had to pick one domain to focus on right now, coding is a very reasonable bet.

r001.rationale: It says better coding can speed up AI research, but does not state that this research then further improves coding capabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes code as a universal interface and action space through which models can use APIs, manipulate data, and interact with the digital world.

r003.rationale: It highlights coding’s clear, verifiable feedback, but does not mention abundant data or say other tool-use settings rarely combine both.

astra-6.text:
I think coding is important for two reasons. First, it’s useful in its own right. A lot of human work involves software, so improving a model’s ability to write, understand, and debug code has a direct practical impact.

Second, coding gives us a concrete way to study how language models can act, rather than just generate text. A model can write a program, run it, observe an error, and revise its approach. That loop—taking an action, getting feedback, and trying again—is central to building agents.

Code also gives us relatively clear feedback. If you generate an essay, judging whether it’s good can be quite subjective. With code, you can often execute it and test whether it does what you intended. Of course, passing tests doesn’t mean you’ve solved every aspect of software engineering, but it gives you a useful signal.

So I see coding both as an important application and as a research environment for developing more general problem-solving abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding is important for two reasons. First, it’s useful in itself. A lot of knowledge work involves software, and helping people write, understand, and maintain code can have a huge impact.

Second, coding gives us a very good environment for studying intelligence. A model can write a program, run it, see an error, and revise its approach. There’s a feedback loop, and we can often check whether the result actually works. That makes it a useful setting for studying reasoning, tool use, and learning from feedback.

And code is more than an output format. It’s a way for a model to act. If you can write and execute code, you can analyze data, automate tasks, and interact with other systems. So progress in coding can help us move from models that answer questions to agents that can carry out more complex tasks.
